I am 76 years old now, and my legs are not what they used to be, but I have farmed this land in Quzhou County for more than fifty years. I never went to school, but I know this soil better than any book. Every household around here grows winter wheat and summer maize in rotation—that is the way of the North China Plain, and I do not see any reason to change it. Last October I sowed my wheat, so it is already in the field. This spring I will irrigate it three more times—at green-up, jointing, and grain filling—and topdress with urea. I will also spray for weeds, aphids, and powdery mildew when my neighbors start spraying, because that is when the pests come. After harvesting the wheat in early June, I will plant hybrid maize the same day or the next; there is no time to waste. For the maize I will sow directly into the wheat stubble without ploughing, which saves labor and fuel. I will give it one round of compound fertilizer at sowing, irrigate once or twice depending on the summer rains, and spray herbicide and insecticide two or three times total. I have four mu of land. It is enough for my wife and me, and any surplus I can sell. I do not grow cotton anymore—it requires too much hand-picking, and my back cannot take it. I also do not trust fancy new crops. Wheat gives me flour, maize gives me feed and cash, and that is all I need.
